written_by_MFA003.Excerpt1: Thirty years ago, my father gave me a small suitcase like the one in this image, filled with his manuscripts, and asked me to read them. I held that suitcase in my hand for a full week, imagining its contents and wavering between the melancholy solitude it would bring and my desire not to disappoint my father. Finally, I decided not to open it because I wanted to remain the child of a father who kept a suitcase of secrets. When my first novel "Cevdet Bey and His Sons" was published in Turkey, I was twenty-three, and I gave it to my father to read. Until then, I had never given him any samples of my writing, and that small suitcase had not yet been mentioned between us. Unlike my mother, my father—who was concerned for my welfare but even more for my freedom—did not object to my becoming a novelist. Like all fathers, he wished for his son to have extraordinary success, yet he refrained from making demands, urging me only to be free and happy.I waited, as nervous as my mother was, for my father's reaction after he had finished reading my novel. Finally, when he returned, overcome with excitement, I studied his expression and searched for clues. My father said not a word, but—ignoring my mother and the others—motioned for me to follow him into his study. For a time, we stood across from each other, like two schoolboys who had quarreled, awkwardly unable to speak. Then, embarrassed by his own emotions, he hugged me. When we pulled apart, he looked at me affectionately and said, "You will be a very good writer, bebeğim." He then added, like a true man of his generation, that he expected me to one day win the prize I am receiving today. I recount this here proudly, yet with some embarrassment—and his supposition has come true.My dear father died in December 2002.
written_by_MFA003.Excerpt2: It was the next night when my father returned to my little apartment and I, anxious for his arrival, waited at the same wobbling card table on which I wrote the unbound novel he held in his hands. It had taken me two years to write it, and in those two years, my mother had refused to read a page. During one of her morning visits over lukewarm tea, she’d said “If it’s writing you want, I fail to see how work in advertising won’t fulfill you.” It was her tone that foretold that in leaping and striving for these dreams, we may lose sight of the path that had been carved for us long before. But my father read the entire novel. He had asked to. And when he slammed the pages onto my table, in the harsh return to the site of their creation, I was certain he would insist I write no more. I allowed myself to believe that, in the moment of silence after the table steadied, my words were so inept they could not draw near the man who best knew me. I believed this until he embraced me. I did not realize until much later, far beyond the glances of accumulated days behind me, that his momentary silence was the struggle for his own words. “One day,” he eventually said. “One day, my son will be a famous author. A Nobel prize author. One day.” The loose pages on the desk were an off-white bond paper, and it is these pages I have kept and oftentimes return to, long after I titled the manuscript Cevdet Bey and His Sons, long after it was sold and published, long after my relocating to a larger apartment in Istanbul and my father’s passing seven years later in December, 2002. I return to the typed and blue-hashed pages not to read but to see what my father had seen, to see him seeing his son and all his promise.

written_by_MFA003.Original: Twenty-three years before my father left me his suitcase, and four years after I had decided, at the age of twenty-two, to become a novelist, and, abandoning all else, shut myself up in a room, I finished my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons.” With trembling hands, I gave my father a typescript of the still unpublished novel, so that he could read it and tell me what he thought. I did this not only because I had confidence in his taste and his intellect; his opinion was very important to me because, unlike my mother, he had not opposed my wish to become a writer. At that point, my father was not with us, but far away. I waited impatiently for his return. When he arrived, two weeks later, I ran to open the door. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.

For a few days, my father refused to talk about the manuscript but later, one cold evening, he expressed a strong and optimistic confidence about my future writing career. Like a proud father he said "Aslanım olacaksın." He didn’t name a prize but he predicted that I would go on to receive a prestigious one. When my father died in 2002, I looked outside the window and imagined that door by which I stood waiting for him and remembered his words of encouragement. Sometimes, when I am alone, I still feel the warmth of that embrace.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: I had given it to him at last, my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons,” and I waited with equal parts fear and excitement for his reaction to it. The book took me several years to complete and the time had not come easily; my mother had not supported the endeavor and took every opportunity to disparage this sodden “waste of youth” while my father quietly, gently, encouraged me with small gifts and an allowance. I knew better than to try convincing my mother, though those modern writers who I hoped to emulate in the West had taken a similar commitment to writing, she did not respect them, and would not want me to achieve a similar goal to any of theirs. I saw my father from across the boiled asphalt lot and felt my fears realized in his step—would he join my mother after reading my manuscript? I rose from my car to meet him. I searched for a hint of his answer in his gait or his eyes and saw nothing but the movements and recognition of an animal. written_by_MFA016.Original: Twenty-three years before my father left me his suitcase, and four years after I had decided, at the age of twenty-two, to become a novelist, and, abandoning all else, shut myself up in a room, I finished my first novel, “Cevdet Bey and His Sons.” With trembling hands, I gave my father a typescript of the still unpublished novel, so that he could read it and tell me what he thought. I did this not only because I had confidence in his taste and his intellect; his opinion was very important to me because, unlike my mother, he had not opposed my wish to become a writer. At that point, my father was not with us, but far away. I waited impatiently for his return. When he arrived, two weeks later, I ran to open the door. My father said nothing, but he immediately threw his arms around me in a way that told me he had liked the book very much. For a while, we were plunged into the sort of awkward silence that often accompanies moments of great emotion. Then, when we had calmed down and begun to talk, my father resorted to highly charged and exaggerated language to express his confidence in me and in my first novel: he told me that one day I would win the prize that I have now received with such great happiness. He said this not because he was trying to convince me of his good opinion or to set the prize as a goal; he said it like a Turkish father, supporting his son, encouraging him by saying, “One day you’ll be a pasha!” For years, whenever he saw me, he would encourage me with the same words.My father died in December, 2002.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. We always thought of ourselves as girls in that place, but we were women in every sense of the word—bleeding and hungry and raging. We couldn’t speak to each other, couldn’t touch each other, couldn’t look Aunt Elizabeth in the eye and especially not Aunt Sara. Every wall was made of concrete and every meal was thin broth. Cold seeped in from everywhere. There were no clocks we were permitted to see, but time passed whenever the Aunts said it did, marching us from chore to chore at the end of their stinging cattle prods. There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. We imagined the Angels releasing us back into the world, a world we were sometimes convinced we’d dreamed up ourselves, a world where we didn’t have to touch our hair to remember what grass felt like. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The smell of the wood chips on the floors of the caged gymnasium where we slept, that stale, sweet odor; the moist sheen of bundled bodies, carried with us into the sunlight. I remember that yearning, that thirst for something we could never grasp. It wasn't just the touch of tongues and fingers, of sweaty thighs; it was a desire for the future. It was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep. We created so many illusions for ourselves, of one kind or another. How else could we live? I remember whispering as we folded laundry late at night, those soft, slow voices moving through the humid air. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the end of the beds. In the semidarkness we could stretch out our arms, when the Aunts weren't looking, and touch each other's hands across space. We learned to lip-read, our heads flat on the beds, turned sideways, watching each other's mouths. In this way we exchanged names, from bed to bed: Alma. Janine. Dolores. Moira. June.The door was locked, and it was forbidden for us to be awake in here after lights-out. We were constantly being watched. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods worn on leather belts, but no guns. Guns were for guards, a.k.a. Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when they were bringing new women or taking the old ones away. They stayed outside, with their backs deliberately turned toward us. They were objects of fear, but familiarity dulled our apprehension. What we fantasized about more than anything else was the possibility of touching them, or having them touch us, using our bodies as the currency, the ultimate coin of exchange—what we would give them for freedom. There was nothing we wouldn't give.

written_by_MFA029.Original: There was old sex in the room and loneliness, and expectation, of something without a shape or name. I remember that yearning, for something that was always about to happen and was never the same as the hands that were on us there and then, in the small of the back, or out back, in the parking lot, or in the television room with the sound turned down and only the pictures flickering over lifting flesh.We yearned for the future. How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? It was in the air; and it was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep, in the army cots that had been set up in rows, with spaces between so we could not talk. We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.

How did we learn it, that talent for insatiability? It was in the air; and it was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep, in the army cots that had been set up in rows, with spaces between so we could not talk. We had flannelette sheets, like children's, and army-issue blankets, old ones that still said U.S. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the ends of the beds. The lights were turned down but not out. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods slung on thongs from their leather belts.No guns though, even they could not be trusted with guns. Guns were for the guards, specially picked from the Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when called, and we weren't allowed out, except for our walks, twice daily, two by two around the football field, which was enclosed now by a chain-link fence topped with barbed wire. The Angels stood outside it with their backs to us. They were objects of fear to us, but of something else as well. If only they would look. If only we could talk to them. Something could be exchanged, we thought, some deal made, some tradeoff, we still had our bodies. That was our fantasy.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Our arms were singed with burns from Aunt Sara’s cattle prod. We always thought of ourselves as girls in that place, but we were women in every sense of the word—bleeding and hungry and raging. We couldn’t speak to each other, couldn’t touch each other, couldn’t look Aunt Elizabeth in the eye and especially not Aunt Sara. Every wall was made of concrete and every meal was thin broth. Cold seeped in from everywhere. There were no clocks we were permitted to see, but time passed whenever the Aunts said it did, marching us from chore to chore at the end of their stinging cattle prods. There was sewing with dull needles and scrubbing floors that refused to get clean and carefully sorting through papers only to have them burned in the incinerator. Our voices shriveled in our throats from lack of use, but our eyes never forgot how to wander. They usually flitted up to the watch towers occupied by the Angels. Their faces were always turned away from us, and whenever we heard gunfire, it was aimed at someone on the outside. We imagined slipping up to the towers, unseen by the Aunts, and pulling down our gray, baggy shifts to reveal our narrow collarbones. We’d once been told this was our best feature. We imagined the Angels releasing us back into the world, a world we were sometimes convinced we’d dreamed up ourselves, a world where we didn’t have to touch our hair to remember what grass felt like. What would happen between the reveal of our bodies and our release was something our imaginations recoiled from, but whatever it might be, we could just keep our eyes closed until it was over, because everything—eventually—was over.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: The smell of the wood chips on the floors of the caged gymnasium where we slept, that stale, sweet odor; the moist sheen of bundled bodies, carried with us into the sunlight. I remember that yearning, that thirst for something we could never grasp. It wasn't just the touch of tongues and fingers, of sweaty thighs; it was a desire for the future. It was still in the air, an afterthought, as we tried to sleep. We created so many illusions for ourselves, of one kind or another. How else could we live? I remember whispering as we folded laundry late at night, those soft, slow voices moving through the humid air. We folded our clothes neatly and laid them on the stools at the end of the beds. In the semidarkness we could stretch out our arms, when the Aunts weren't looking, and touch each other's hands across space. We learned to lip-read, our heads flat on the beds, turned sideways, watching each other's mouths. In this way we exchanged names, from bed to bed: Alma. Janine. Dolores. Moira. June.The door was locked, and it was forbidden for us to be awake in here after lights-out. We were constantly being watched. Aunt Sara and Aunt Elizabeth patrolled; they had electric cattle prods worn on leather belts, but no guns. Guns were for guards, a.k.a. Angels. The guards weren't allowed inside the building except when they were bringing new women or taking the old ones away. They stayed outside, with their backs deliberately turned toward us. They were objects of fear, but familiarity dulled our apprehension. What we fantasized about more than anything else was the possibility of touching them, or having them touch us, using our bodies as the currency, the ultimate coin of exchange—what we would give them for freedom. There was nothing we wouldn't give.

written_by_MFA004.Excerpt2: Even their names were duplicitous, Aunt Sara and Elizabeth. Aunt Sara evoked the image of a mousy-haired woman who hoarded loose buttons and bright thread in a cookie tin. Elizabeth sounded like the gold-tressed protagonist of an Austen novel who was ferocious on horseback, meek in conversation, entitled to marry well. They carried cattle prods and the first time I’d seen one, gripped in Elizabeth’s wide hand, I’d sniffed the compound for a mealy smell of animals but was met with fecund whiffs of soil and the tart odor of women under stress. Holly, Rozalyn, and I were middle-age with new wrinkles yet cloistered and monitored like boarding school miscreants. We had a box of a room with pocked floors and standard bunk-beds, blue sheets that reminded of a hospital and not the sky. And where was the fourth girl, smart-mouthed Sara? She’d talked back at gender studies that morning, suggesting a definition of women that was beyond the womb. Sara had too much ambition and ambition was what the cattle prods corrected. Outside our picture-book sized window was a big square of yellow grass and men with guns who called themselves Angels. My favorite guard had a roman nose and thick, tan neck. I imagined that if I got close enough, I could lave my tongue, cat-like, up his neck. I was convinced he’d love me just from this, from those few seconds of wet, lancing heat. He’d take me in his arms and run me to freedom. At twilight, he liked to shoot at the crows in the sky. With that rain of holy fire escaping his gun, he looked blessed and impossible to crucify, an angel indeed.

We imagine what it would be like to go to them, to touch their arms and their chests and their beards, to take off our clothes and show them our warm bodies, watch their faces unthaw at the sight of our soft and supple skin. We imagine what it would be like to leave the cold, fetid horror of this place behind, let it become a memory, a vile, coppery taste at the backs of our throats. For now, we sit and we watch. We stay still and we dream and we yearn. We wait and we imagine something other than the rigid darkness of today.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. It wouldn’t, said Marianne. You’d be wonderful. Really. She thought about them as two plants, sharing the same soil, growing toward the light together. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? Connell looked at her and wiped a tear from the top of his lip. He seemed to understand. He nodded like he did, and the corner of his mouth betrayed the hint of a smile. People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. The rain was getting softer, and it seemed like it would stop very soon. She felt that she was looking at the future, a wavy, edgeless thing, grey with little speckles of light.

written_by_MFA008.Original: That's ridiculous, he says. I'm not going to New York without you. I wouldn't even be here if it wasn't for you.It's true, she thinks, he wouldn’t be. He would be somewhere else entirely, living a different kind of life. He would be different with women even, and his aspirations for love would be different. Really, she thinks, really. People can really change one another.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. It wouldn’t, said Marianne. You’d be wonderful. Really. She thought about them as two plants, sharing the same soil, growing toward the light together. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? Connell looked at her and wiped a tear from the top of his lip. He seemed to understand. He nodded like he did, and the corner of his mouth betrayed the hint of a smile. People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. The rain was getting softer, and it seemed like it would stop very soon. She felt that she was looking at the future, a wavy, edgeless thing, grey with little speckles of light.

written_by_MFA008.Original: That's ridiculous, he says. I'm not going to New York without you. I wouldn't even be here if it wasn't for you.It's true, she thinks, he wouldn’t be. He would be somewhere else entirely, living a different kind of life. He would be different with women even, and his aspirations for love would be different. And Marianne herself, she would be another person completely. Would she ever have been happy? And what kind of happiness might it have been? All these years they've been like two little plants sharing the same plot of soil, growing around one another, contorting to make room, taking certain unlikely positions. But in the end she has done something for him, she’s made a new life possible, and she can always feel good about that. I'd miss you too much, he says. I’d be sick, honestly. At first. But it would get better. They sit in silence now, Marianne moving the brush methodically through her hair, feeling for knots and slowly, patiently untangling them. There's no point in being impatient anymore. You know I love you, says Connell. I'm never going to feel the same way for someone else. She nods, okay. He's telling the truth. To be honest, I don’t know what to do, he says. Say you want me to stay and I will. She closes her eyes. He probably won’t come back, she thinks. Or he will, differently. What they have now they can never have back again. But for her the pain of loneliness will be nothing to the pain that she used to feel, of being unworthy. He brought her goodness like a gift and now it belongs to her. Meanwhile his life opens out before him in all directions at once. They’ve done a lot of good for each other. Really, she thinks, really. People can really change one another.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.
written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: Connell chewed at the tip of his finger. I can tell you’re feeling anxious, said Marianne. Why wouldn’t I be, said Connell. It’s a big thing, isn’t it? Yeah, said Marianne. It is. It’s a really big thing. I know. She wrapped her cardigan tighter around herself. It was cold in the room. Connell fidgeted. He sat on his hands and rocked back and forth, then said: It would be hard. Leaving all this. I won’t have the life that I have with you. It would be a half-life or something. It wouldn’t, said Marianne. You’d be wonderful. Really. She thought about them as two plants, sharing the same soil, growing toward the light together. She knew they would not be the same after they parted from each other, but that things would be all right. She looked out the window as big drops of rain came down, one after the other, flattening themselves against the glass. Connell wiped his nose on his sleeve. His eyes were pink. Marianne thought about it, what it would really be like. Connell would uproot out of the soil, their soil, and he would go somewhere new. And, while Marianne would miss him, and perhaps feel lonely, she would never feel unworthy again. She said, out loud: That’s something you can’t take away, isn't it? Connell looked at her and wiped a tear from the top of his lip. He seemed to understand. He nodded like he did, and the corner of his mouth betrayed the hint of a smile. People can change each other, Marianne thought, and it was true. They can really change each other. She looked out the window again. The rain was getting softer, and it seemed like it would stop very soon. She felt that she was looking at the future, a wavy, edgeless thing, grey with little speckles of light.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: Remember how different we were when we first met, Connell said. Marianne paused, face warmed by his shoulder. She thought that perhaps they were at the sort of height one jumps from and survives jumping from, that she would, despite the loneliness, be able to carry on from this: two plants sharing a large pot, space and light made for them both as their stems grew in opposite directions. Often she felt this way with her friends. Sometimes young friendships to her seemed featherweight and passing, and even in the depths of real connection, these relationships felt unimportant and survivable. Survivable, she meant, if they ended. But with Connell, she would not really survive losing him forever. Marianne could not imagine for them any real or permanent parting, nothing as serious as death. This moment between them was unlike that unfathomable permanence and unlike how she felt with friends, and bearable for it. She told him this.You've been the person who shaped my life, really, Connell said, who I am today. She shrugged against him and felt sick to imagine them parted but could see in that possibility an uncertain future that took nothing from their certain past. You were the first person to really see me, she said, and then laughed at herself, insecure. In this way, pieces of their early dynamic still clung to her: a certain unsteadiness that sometimes made her mean but never cruel. A feeling, perhaps, that despite all they had meant to each other, there was some part of her still unworthy and always seeking more of him. But Connell smoothed her hair and sighed, his inhaling chest elevating hers, and said sadly, We were made to make each other into adults, I think. For a moment they, attached to each other, shared breath in an afternoon marked by parting but not only by sadness.

written_by_MFA011.Original: That's ridiculous, he says. I'm not going to New York without you. I wouldn't even be here if it wasn't for you.It's true, she thinks, he wouldn’t be. He would be somewhere else entirely, living a different kind of life. He would be different with women even, and his aspirations for love would be different. And Marianne herself, she would be another person completely. Would she ever have been happy? And what kind of happiness might it have been? All these years they've been like two little plants sharing the same plot of soil, growing around one another, contorting to make room, taking certain unlikely positions. But in the end she has done something for him, she’s made a new life possible, and she can always feel good about that. I'd miss you too much, he says. I’d be sick, honestly. At first. But it would get better. They sit in silence now, Marianne moving the brush methodically through her hair, feeling for knots and slowly, patiently untangling them. There's no point in being impatient anymore. You know I love you, says Connell. I'm never going to feel the same way for someone else. She nods, okay. He's telling the truth. To be honest, I don’t know what to do, he says. Say you want me to stay and I will. She closes her eyes. He probably won’t come back, she thinks. Or he will, differently. What they have now they can never have back again. But for her the pain of loneliness will be nothing to the pain that she used to feel, of being unworthy. He brought her goodness like a gift and now it belongs to her. Meanwhile his life opens out before him in all directions at once. They’ve done a lot of good for each other. Really, she thinks, really. People can really change one another.

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: You know, he says, it’s going to be really hard for me to be apart from you, Marianne. Like, I literally don’t think I would have had the life I’ve had without you. Marianne smiles and looks down at the floor, where a puddle of water has formed from the snow in an obscure shape. She thinks about the first night she met Connell, the kiss they shared atop the washing machine in his mother’s house, and says, My life obviously wouldn’t be the same, either. You’ve done so much for me, really. When we first met, that first night at the house, I felt like I wasn’t worth anything to anyone. To be honest, there were nights when I might’ve wished I was dead. But you saw me, and you changed the way I saw myself. You’ve given me something that I didn’t even know was possible. Connell chuckles and wipes away with his shirtsleeve at a tear that has formed at the corner of his eye. I’m not sure I would know what it’s like to be seen without you, she continues. We’re sort of like two plants that have shared the same soil for their whole lives, always growing around each other without realizing it. But even though we’ve done so much good for each other, I know that things change and that we can’t control what will happen in the future. As she speaks, Marianne knows that things may never be the same between herself and Connell. She remembers again that first night in the house and the feeling of his warm lips on her ear, then imagines coming home to an empty house each night, with no one to leave empty mugs of tea out drying on the big windowsill overlooking the park. To be without him is almost unimaginable; then again, loneliness, she thinks, is a small price to pay for Connell’s happiness.
written_by_MFA011.Excerpt2: Marianne says nothing for a time. Her arm, his arm, her leg. Maybe we could, if it’s just going to be a year, she says. Don’t think other people have gone through life without having long periods of time on their own, you know. Yes, he says. I just love you so much. I know, she says. I love you too. He nods, breathing in. Her large dark eyes are like openings to something. Without you I would be nothing, he says. I would just be a shadow walking around the town. I saw you, I really saw you. I wanted you to exist here and be happy. Anyway, he says. I believe we have done a lot of good for each other. Yes. I know. It’s sad because it was the happiest time of her life, and it’s over now. Never again will she have what she had then, the love and care of another person. Never again will they be two plants sharing the same soil, one leaning in the light, the other languishing in the shade. She doesn’t blame him, she no longer believes her unhappiness is inevitable. No one can be what another person wants them to be. But she adds: You should go, if you want to. I’ll always be here. You know that. Does she think it’s possible to belong to someone this way? So concretely, so unquestionably. To have someone belong to you. The scene could still unite them, for those minutes, so that it would be unthinkable to be separated from him again, unthinkable that they had wasted so long already. But she knows he won’t be confused about what he has to do with his life. She knows he’ll go and she’ll stay, and that’s how it will be. People can really change one another. You should go, she says. I’ll always be here.

written_by_MFA016.Excerpt1: We sat there, my father and I, at the group table. Anyone looking our way could see our discomfort. I touched my spectacles and watched myself in the great wall mirror - each time finding myself paler and more repulsive. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: The restaurant was an annex to the Trois-Couronnes.I had a pale face and was wearing my spectacles that day, which made me look sad. That wasn't the issue, though. My father and I had been seated at the table reserved for groups, on the far side of the dining room, and were ignored throughout the meal. At the next table, there was a man with his daughter, who was older than I was, maybe seventeen, sleek and tanned with short blonde hair. I remember a long, gilt-framed mirror hanging above their heads, reflecting endless repetitions of identical people. The girl talked confidently to her father and laughingly spooned up her yogurt. In those days, I didn't know what yogurt was. She seemed at home, oblivious to her surroundings, wearing no jacket or headscarf, simply her checkered summer dress. She made me feel awkward and ashamed, although I couldn't explain why, my only desire being to leave as soon as possible. Later on, walking along the streets, my father kept saying, "Those mashed potatoes looked like pig slop." For the first time, I realized that he had been marking time to continue, repeating the reason why he hadn't eaten anything on his plate. I didn't think of asking him what difference it made what the potatoes looked like. Deep down, he was upset at being treated as a second-class customer just because we weren't dining "à la carte" like the people sitting near us.

written_by_MFA016.Original: One evening ‒ it was our last day ‒ in Tours, we had dinner in a brightly-lit restaurant where the walls were lined with mirrors, frequented by a sophisticated clientele. My father and I were seated at the end of a long table set up for the group. The waiters were paying little attention to us; we had to wait a long time between courses. At a small table nearby sat a girl aged fourteen or fifteen, suntanned, in a low-cut dress, and an elderly man who appeared to be her father.They were talking and laughing quite freely, completely at ease, oblivious of other people. She was dipping into a thick milky substance in a glass ‒ some years later I learnt this was yogurt, which people like us had never heard of. I caught sight of myself in the mirror, pale and sad-looking with my spectacles, silently sitting beside my father, who was staring into the far distance. I could see everything that separated me from that girl yet I wouldn’t have known what to do to resemble her.Afterward, my father complained with unusual vehemence about this restaurant, where he claimed we had been served mashed potatoes made with “pig slop,” white and tasteless. Several weeks later, he was still venting his anger over the meal and its disgraceful “pig slop.” Although he never actually said so ‒ it was probably then that I began decoding his speech ‒ it was his way of expressing resentment at having been treated with contempt because we were not chic customers who ate “à la carte.”

My father and I were seated at the end of a long table set up for the group. The waiters were paying little attention to us; we had to wait a long time between courses. At a small table nearby sat a girl aged fourteen or fifteen, suntanned, in a low-cut dress, and an elderly man who appeared to be her father.They were talking and laughing quite freely, completely at ease, oblivious of other people. My father grew more agitated, too, letting our meager conversation drop, because the waiter had still not come with his mashed potatoes after so many dreary minutes. I watched a girl near my age across the room dining at her own special table with an older man. I watched her through the mirror in case she might meet my eye. She was tan and lifted a spoon of creamy yogurt to her lips. I was lost, for a moment, in imagining its flavor. I had never tasted yogurt before. When our food came at last, it looked nothing like the pretty plate in front of the tan girl - the same way my clothes looked nothing like hers - the same way my skin matched the grey sky outside while hers glowed like the sun in the tropics. Later, in the streets and at home, my father repeatedly talked about the "pig slop" they served him at the restaurant and vowed never to return. It took me years to understand how he was complaining - in his own way - of the hurt that came with seeing, but never ordering, "à la carte."
written_by_MFA016.Excerpt2: The restaurant was an annex to the Trois-Couronnes.I had a pale face and was wearing my spectacles that day, which made me look sad. That wasn't the issue, though. My father and I had been seated at the table reserved for groups, on the far side of the dining room, and were ignored throughout the meal. At the next table, there was a man with his daughter, who was older than I was, maybe seventeen, sleek and tanned with short blonde hair. I remember a long, gilt-framed mirror hanging above their heads, reflecting endless repetitions of identical people. The girl talked confidently to her father and laughingly spooned up her yogurt. In those days, I didn't know what yogurt was. She seemed at home, oblivious to her surroundings, wearing no jacket or headscarf, simply her checkered summer dress. She made me feel awkward and ashamed, although I couldn't explain why, my only desire being to leave as soon as possible. Later on, walking along the streets, my father kept saying, "Those mashed potatoes looked like pig slop." For the first time, I realized that he had been marking time to continue, repeating the reason why he hadn't eaten anything on his plate. I didn't think of asking him what difference it made what the potatoes looked like. Deep down, he was upset at being treated as a second-class customer just because we weren't dining "à la carte" like the people sitting near us.
written_by_MFA016.Reason: Excerpt 1 states things more explicitly than the original (e.g. "touched my spectacles" and "imagining its flavor" instead of discovering yogurt later), therefore it feels mismatched in tone. Excerpt 2 has a different time line but in terms of word choice, tone and flow, it is much closer to the original.
written_by_MFA016.Original: One evening ‒ it was our last day ‒ in Tours, we had dinner in a brightly-lit restaurant where the walls were lined with mirrors, frequented by a sophisticated clientele. My father and I were seated at the end of a long table set up for the group. The waiters were paying little attention to us; we had to wait a long time between courses. At a small table nearby sat a girl aged fourteen or fifteen, suntanned, in a low-cut dress, and an elderly man who appeared to be her father.They were talking and laughing quite freely, completely at ease, oblivious of other people. She was dipping into a thick milky substance in a glass ‒ some years later I learnt this was yogurt, which people like us had never heard of. I caught sight of myself in the mirror, pale and sad-looking with my spectacles, silently sitting beside my father, who was staring into the far distance. I could see everything that separated me from that girl yet I wouldn’t have known what to do to resemble her.Afterward, my father complained with unusual vehemence about this restaurant, where he claimed we had been served mashed potatoes made with “pig slop,” white and tasteless. Several weeks later, he was still venting his anger over the meal and its disgraceful “pig slop.” Although he never actually said so ‒ it was probably then that I began decoding his speech ‒ it was his way of expressing resentment at having been treated with contempt because we were not chic customers who ate “à la carte.”

written_by_MFA011.Excerpt1: My father and I dined at an upscale restaurant in the 13th arrondissement. We each ordered chicken legs and mashed potatoes, and we sat stiffly while waiting for our food. It was clear that both of us felt uncomfortable with the opulence of the space, but neither of us knew how to say so. Nearby, a girl around the age of fifteen sat with an older man, presumably her father, eating a foreign-looking food that I didn't recognize—a bowl of yogurt, I later learned. She looked deeply at ease eating her meal, and I was disturbed to see myself in the mirror on the adjacent wall—spectacled, pale. Compared to the girl, I looked homely and unimportant, or at least I felt that I did at the time. For a moment I imagined myself as the girl, tan and comfortable among the trappings of wealth, though even then I knew that the hallmarks of the working class were written all over my face and my behavior. My father and I sat for a while in silence, and when the waitstaff brought out our plates, he remarked to me that his mashed potatoes looked like "pig slop." At the time, I thought he was just being fussy about his meal and I felt annoyed. Later I understood that he was deeply hurt at having been treated as second-class citizens who weren't ordering à la carte like the girl and her father, though he never said as much—he just continued talking about the potatoes, their unpleasant texture, their unsightly gray appearance.

written_by_MFA033.Excerpt1: My father wanted to take me to lunch. He found a restaurant unlike any I’d ever been to, unlike anything that existed in C. Any excitement I felt disappeared quickly. We had been treated as second-class citizens because we ordered the prix fixe, instead of selecting expensive dishes à la carte like the more sophisticated clientele. I wanted to forget about it. If we didn’t speak of the event, then perhaps it wasn’t real.

written_by_MFA009.Excerpt1: It was Saint Patrick's Day, though in her room there was no evidence of that. The world outside her window was still just ice-crusted heaps of snow and muddy patches. The sunlight reflected off them and whooshed in, bursting onto her ceiling. A tray with a small bowl of wobbly green Jell-O sat on a table over her bed, uneaten. My mother's arms lay on top of the blanket, waxy and unrecognizable to me now. I sat beside her, holding her hands, kissing them. She didn't seem to register that I was there anymore, though she was not asleep. She would not allow herself to sleep. Her eyes were wide open and still wildly, unquestionably, irrepressibly blue. Bluer than the sky. Bluer than the enamel-blue tulip-shaped pot that Bruce would get in the mail a few days later. Bluer than the water I'd swum across. Her eyes were the bluest balls of fire, and throughout those three weeks they blazed at me—bitter, bewildered, desolate, honest, true—and then the last six days, as she bore down to refuse sleep, they shifted to a blue that was so quiet, so heroically faithful, so fucking insistent. Insistent upon what, I didn't know. Her will, I supposed. To live.
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt2: It is one thing to know something and another other thing to live it. I knew that my mother would eventually leave. All of us eventually leave. I knew that it would be hard. It was Saint Patrick’s day. I’d brought her a green cup of Jell-O, which of course she didn’t eat. When she died, I had stepped into the bathroom. I was in the shower, running water through my hair. What a ridiculous place to be when someone dies. It wasn’t that I thought there would be some movie-scene ending. That she would wait to go until I was holding her hand, looking into her eyes. That death itself would wait until I could walk her to its door and burn with her until her fire turned to smoke and her sparkling blue eyes flipped through the stages of departure. From anger to confusion to something like heroism, the whispering heroism we all embody when we face our last moment. A heroism shining in the blue of her eyes, a deep, flickering blue which proclaimed how much she wanted to stay, here, with the rest of us, even as she left. I knew, after all, that death didn’t wait for anyone. And yet, no matter how much I thought I knew, when she went, what did I find myself shouting in my head? What other than “wait”?

written_by_MFA009.Original: I watched my mother. It was March, and outside, the sun glinted off the sidewalks and the icy edges of the snow. It was Saint Patrick’s Day and the nurses brought my mother a square block of green Jell-O that sat quivering on the table beside her. It was the last full day of her life, and my mother did not sleep, she did not wake. She held her eyes still and open. They were the bluest thing in the room, perhaps in all of Duluth. Bluer than the lake. They were the color of the sky on the best day of your life.My mother died fast but not all of a sudden. A slow-burning fire when flames disappear to smoke and then smoke to air. Blue, blue eyes. Daggers of blue wanting and wanting. To stay, to stay.

written_by_MFA012.Original: I watched my mother. It was March, and outside, the sun glinted off the sidewalks and the icy edges of the snow. It was Saint Patrick’s Day and the nurses brought my mother a square block of green Jell-O that sat quivering on the table beside her. It was the last full day of her life, and my mother did not sleep, she did not wake. She held her eyes still and open. They were the bluest thing in the room, perhaps in all of Duluth. Bluer than the lake. They were the color of the sky on the best day of your life.My mother died fast but not all of a sudden. A slow-burning fire when flames disappear to smoke and then smoke to air. She never once closed her eyes. First they were bitter and then they were bewildered and then they changed again to something else, to a state that I have had, finally, to see as heroic. Blue, blue eyes. Daggers of blue wanting and wanting. To stay, to stay.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: On March 17th, the world was green, but my mother’s eyes were blue. Blue as the sky in early spring. Blue as the Joni Mitchell album. Blue as the bitterness within them, my mother’s undefeated eyes. I was losing her, on that snowy day in spring. Yet she didn’t try to sleep, she didn’t give in, she didn’t snuff out the inner fire of her. She gazed out the window, bewildered by the partiers, the people dressed for Saint Patrick’s Day. The city streets were alive with voices. Sunlight danced along the surface of the Jell-O. She didn’t eat, she just looked at it, that fucking glob of green. And when she looked away, I knew she would die. Her fire had burned away. All the years of shattered sparks and roaring flame and now she was only ashes. Twin flames burning low. I hadn’t always loved my mother in life. We had had our difficulties, that was for damn sure. But as she lay on that bed, showing the blue steel of her eyes, I knew what my mother was. She was a hero. She was a fighter. She was the strongest woman I’ve known. Her lips moved a little, and I leaned in close. Grasping for her life, she slipped away.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: It was Saint Patrick's Day, though in her room there was no evidence of that. The world outside her window was still just ice-crusted heaps of snow and muddy patches. The sunlight reflected off them and whooshed in, bursting onto her ceiling. A tray with a small bowl of wobbly green Jell-O sat on a table over her bed, uneaten. My mother's arms lay on top of the blanket, waxy and unrecognizable to me now. I sat beside her, holding her hands, kissing them. She didn't seem to register that I was there anymore, though she was not asleep. She would not allow herself to sleep. Her eyes were wide open and still wildly, unquestionably, irrepressibly blue. Bluer than the sky. Bluer than the enamel-blue tulip-shaped pot that Bruce would get in the mail a few days later. Bluer than the water I'd swum across. Her eyes were the bluest balls of fire, and throughout those three weeks they blazed at me—bitter, bewildered, desolate, honest, true—and then the last six days, as she bore down to refuse sleep, they shifted to a blue that was so quiet, so heroically faithful, so fucking insistent. Insistent upon what, I didn't know. Her will, I supposed. To live.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.

written_by_MFA029.Original: I watched my mother. It was March, and outside, the sun glinted off the sidewalks and the icy edges of the snow. It was Saint Patrick’s Day and the nurses brought my mother a square block of green Jell-O that sat quivering on the table beside her. It was the last full day of her life, and my mother did not sleep, she did not wake. She held her eyes still and open. They were the bluest thing in the room, perhaps in all of Duluth. Bluer than the lake. They were the color of the sky on the best day of your life.My mother died fast but not all of a sudden. A slow-burning fire when flames disappear to smoke and then smoke to air. She never once closed her eyes. First they were bitter and then they were bewildered and then they changed again to something else, to a state that I have had, finally, to see as heroic. Blue, blue eyes. Daggers of blue wanting and wanting. To stay, to stay.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: My mother died on St. Patrick’s Day. There was snow outside, and sunlight glanced off the ice and back into her hospital room. A cup of green Jell-O lingered untouched on its tray. My mother was unresponsive, but not quite asleep. Her eyes were open and vivid. There was an alertness in them still, but what she was looking at, I could not say. The bright blue of her irises was like a frozen lake, contrasting the dull wash of beige and gray shrouding the room. The sky lived inside my mother. It lived inside her then, too, even as we bided time together at the very end, knowing there was only one thing left for her to do. Her fading life was a fire flickering down to smoke—it would only last as long as there was something to burn. There was bitterness too in her eyes, then bewilderment, then a stoic, quiet heroism. A commitment to her own dignity. A promise to endure this final test, no matter how unfairly it had been imposed on her. Her eyes were so blue, my mother’s eyes, a fierce blue, a frozen lake, a sheen of ice that refused to melt, even as the sun broke it apart.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: It was Saint Patrick's Day, though in her room there was no evidence of that. The world outside her window was still just ice-crusted heaps of snow and muddy patches. The sunlight reflected off them and whooshed in, bursting onto her ceiling. A tray with a small bowl of wobbly green Jell-O sat on a table over her bed, uneaten. My mother's arms lay on top of the blanket, waxy and unrecognizable to me now. I sat beside her, holding her hands, kissing them. She didn't seem to register that I was there anymore, though she was not asleep. She would not allow herself to sleep. Her eyes were wide open and still wildly, unquestionably, irrepressibly blue. Bluer than the sky. Bluer than the enamel-blue tulip-shaped pot that Bruce would get in the mail a few days later. Bluer than the water I'd swum across. Her eyes were the bluest balls of fire, and throughout those three weeks they blazed at me—bitter, bewildered, desolate, honest, true—and then the last six days, as she bore down to refuse sleep, they shifted to a blue that was so quiet, so heroically faithful, so fucking insistent. Insistent upon what, I didn't know. Her will, I supposed. To live.

Senior and Junior, two very old men, opened their eyes in their bedrooms on the fourth floor of a sea-green building on a leafy lane, just out of sight of Elliot’s Beach, where, that evening, the young would congregate, as they always did, to perform the rites of youth, not far from the village of the fisherfolk, who had no time for such frivolity. written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: One morning in a town quite near Chennai, the sun arose with a ferocity and began beating down on the town's residents, and there was no time to blink back dawn, the children were already awake and fussing for food, and Miss Aadhya had started on the first pot of coffee, and from her window she could hear Bollywood music, already blaring, and below her the old man whose name no one knew was praying, and above her, on the fourth floor of the Aquamarine building, Senior struggled against that veil that separates dream from reality, and broke through, and was awake. At the same time, his neighbor, Junior, awoke. The two men's eyes opened at the same time. Kabir was now calling to his friends, everyone making plans for an evening at the Elliot’s beach, the promise of cool water the only thing making it bearable to get through the hot afternoon. All the members of the town were connected to each other, as a marionette has strings attached to each of its joints, each small movement producing an equal and opposite reaction. Senior swung his legs out of bed and Junior finished brushing his teeth. The clamor of the town stirred something in both of them, and, with one elegant pull, they both lifted their heads and decided to go out, onto their own veranda.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: The day heated up and we heard the prayer bells in the temples, the bhangra beats from the music trucks plying their enthusiastic trade, the untuneful crying of children. It was time for coffee, and coffee, and coffee yet again, and lemon rice garnished with fried cashews, and all the other wondrous concoctions on offer in Madras. The two old men on the fourth floor of their sea-green building were released from their rooms by the day off like ships slipping their moorings, but they were rusty and they didn't go very far. Their names were blazoned across mailboxes and doorbells. Crowds of the young were descending upon Elliot's Beach, young men in cricket gear, young women deep in laughter and high fragrance, lovers hating their separation; and bikes, bikes, bikes. The sea was a water lily, the young people there were bees. Just a few short years ago Senior and Junior would have been down there too, scampering with the best, but now they had their own slow dance. They woke up just before noon and put on their two-day-old clothes. As if, by some mysterious machinery of fate, the timing wheels within their thickening, aging frames had been perfectly synchronized, they stepped out onto their verandahs at almost the same precise second and stood looking out into the world.

The aroma of filter coffee boiled up from the terraces of the cafes, which were filled with tourists from Tuscany, Madrid, Tyrol. In other neighborhoods, children rendezvoused with their peers in shady alleyways, holding tense diplomatic summits over their games of tag. The heat lingered over the city like a sinister spirit cavalry, a battalion of jinns casting spells over Elliot’s Beach; over the twin harbors and colonial promenade; over the government center and the inland districts; and back out again to one sea-green apartment building, on the fourth floor of which there were two empty verandahs. In the corresponding room, two men simultaneously awakened from their afternoon naps and stepped out onto these verandahs, which it should be said were no longer empty. Senior and Junior, as the men were called by their respective acquaintances, did not look at each other; nor did they watch the youth wander lazily from the streets to the promenade, passing marijuana cigarettes down the line like the world’s slowest relay team. Senior and Junior looked out at Elliot’s Beach, this strange sandy coin that had been cast away by fate.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: The day heated up and we heard the prayer bells in the temples, the bhangra beats from the music trucks plying their enthusiastic trade, the untuneful crying of children. It was time for coffee, and coffee, and coffee yet again, and lemon rice garnished with fried cashews, and all the other wondrous concoctions on offer in Madras. The two old men on the fourth floor of their sea-green building were released from their rooms by the day off like ships slipping their moorings, but they were rusty and they didn't go very far. Their names were blazoned across mailboxes and doorbells. Crowds of the young were descending upon Elliot's Beach, young men in cricket gear, young women deep in laughter and high fragrance, lovers hating their separation; and bikes, bikes, bikes. The sea was a water lily, the young people there were bees. Just a few short years ago Senior and Junior would have been down there too, scampering with the best, but now they had their own slow dance. They woke up just before noon and put on their two-day-old clothes. As if, by some mysterious machinery of fate, the timing wheels within their thickening, aging frames had been perfectly synchronized, they stepped out onto their verandahs at almost the same precise second and stood looking out into the world.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: There are several small details in excerpt 2 that match the original paragraph, particularly the ending. Obviously the original makes no mention of the coffee or food but it's the small details that make me feel as though excerpt 2 is slightly more similar to the original than excerpt 1.
written_by_MFA012.Original: The day that Junior fell down began like any other day: the explosion of heat rippling the air, the trumpeting sunlight, the traffic’s tidal surges, the prayer chants in the distance, the cheap film music rising from the floor below, the loud pelvic thrusts of an 'item number' dancing across a neighbor’s TV, a child’s cry, a mother’s rebuke, unexplained laughter, scarlet expectorations, bicycles, the newly plaited hair of schoolgirls, the smell of strong sweet coffee, a green wing flashing in a tree. Senior and Junior, two very old men, opened their eyes in their bedrooms on the fourth floor of a sea-green building on a leafy lane, just out of sight of Elliot’s Beach, where, that evening, the young would congregate, as they always did, to perform the rites of youth, not far from the village of the fisherfolk, who had no time for such frivolity. The poor were puritans by night and day. As for the old, they had rites of their own and did not need to wait for evening. With the sun stabbing at them through their window blinds, the two old men struggled to their feet and lurched out onto their adjacent verandas, emerging at almost the same moment, like characters in an ancient tale, trapped in fateful coincidences, unable to escape the consequences of chance.

written_by_MFA010.Excerpt1: That year, at Christmas, my father gave me three crisp hundred-dollar bills instead of a gift. He invited me to join him and Chitra and Rupa and Piu at Disney World, where they were planning to spend part of the girls' winter vacation. I told him I couldn't go because school started up again the day after New Year's, but I didn't tell him that I checked the calendar first and realized that we would be back in plenty of time. To make up for it, I bought my half sisters ridiculously expensive presents—a record player for Rupa and a camera for Piu. Rupa cried when I told her I wasn't going to Disney World, which was where the record player and camera would be put to use. Piu put her arms around me. "I don't understand you, Didi," she said, still in her small, high voice. "What did we do wrong that makes you not want to go?" The truth was that in my eyes they had done nothing wrong, whereas I was punished by their mere existence. But I was still convinced that it was up to me to honor my mother's memory, just as they instinctively honored the man who was their father but not really mine. Still, I sensed that Chitra was relieved by my decision, and, by extension, so was my father.
written_by_MFA010.Excerpt2: I was home during winter. On Christmas morning, my father entered my room with a thin, white envelope in hand. Inside, there were ten twenty-dollar notes, totalling a sum of two hundred dollars, the most generous amount I had ever received from my father. I thanked him profusely, but it seemed like a prologue to the real question my father wanted to ask me. He invited me to Disney World, where he was planning to take Chitra, his new wife, and my two half-sisters, Rupa and Piu, during spring break. But I felt distant from his new family, like a string being pulled from both ends. I fabricated some excuse about having to be on-campus during that time since I was a Resident Assistant, and declined his invitation. Later that week, as we sat on the floor circled around the Christmas tree in our living room, Rupa and Piu expressed their disappointment. They could not understand why I would not want to join them in Disney World. "It's Disney World," they exclaimed. But I kept thinking of my late mother, and everything I owed her. I felt a responsibility to hold back, to stay with her memory, as if her place in our family was still untouched and unoccupied, in the same way that Rupa and Piu symbolized and remained committed to their father’s legacy. Besides, I felt, with a strange ease, that Chitra and my father, too, were relieved by my decision to leave the four of them alone to enjoy their holiday.
written_by_MFA010.Reason: Neither example gets the amount of money given correctly - $300 in excerpt 1 and $200 in excerpt 2. Other than that both excerpts do a good job of replicating the original. Both assume that the two girls are the narrators half sisters and that Chitra and his dad are married. I think excerpt 1 just shades it, as it refers to the presents for the girls, interpreting these as being a camera and record player.
written_by_MFA010.Original: For Christmas, my father bought me a sweater and a shirt, but later he gave me an envelope containing ten hundred-dollar bills. “You will need it for this and that,” he said when I told him it was too much. My father had also arranged to go to Disney World for five days; this, along with the toys under the tree, was his present to the girls. “You are welcome to join us,” my father said when he announced this news on Christmas morning, but I said no, making up something about there being a winter session at Swarthmore. My father did not try to persuade me. But Rupa and Piu were devastated. “Why don’t you want to come?” they kept asking, all the more bewildered when they discovered that I had never been to Disney World. I sensed that they needed me, as I needed them, to mask the growing, incontrovertible fact that Chitra and my father now formed a couple. My presence was proof that my mother had once existed, just as they represented the physical legacy of their dead father. “Won’t you be lonely by yourself?” Chitra asked me more than once. At the same time, I gathered that she, like my father, was relieved to hear my plans. I had no plans, of course, other than to be in the house alone.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.
written_by_MFA015.Reason: Excerpt 1 is closer to the original in voice and style. It matches the calm, reflective tone and controlled emotion of the original better than Excerpt 2, which feels more active and emotionally charged. Both of these excerpts are very similar to the original and difficult to separate, but the first is closer.
written_by_MFA015.Original: That was the only time, as I stood there, looking at that strange rubbish, feeling the wind coming across those empty fields, that I started to imagine just a little fantasy thing, because this was Norfolk after all, and it was only a couple of weeks since I’d lost him. I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.

I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shore-line of odd stuff caught along the fencing, and I half-closed my eyes and imagined this was the spot where everything I'd ever lost since my childhood had washed up, and I was now standing here in front of it, and if I waited long enough, a tiny figure would appear on the horizon across the field, and gradually get larger until I'd see it was Tommy, and he'd wave, maybe even call. The fantasy never got beyond that --I didn't let it-- and though the tears rolled down my face, I wasn't sobbing or out of control. I just waited a bit, then turned back to the car, to drive off to wherever it was I was supposed to be.

written_by_MFA015.Excerpt1: There once existed a time here, I suppose, when I could walk this windswept field without knocking my feet against all that came before. But now the world has filled it up with itself. Children’s playthings that were surely once my own, kites wrapped around a wayward branch, brought here as if they’d always been. Because maybe they always had. It gets so I can see Tommy now, coming up over the hillside, waving at me the way he used to––as if I was all he wanted and could want out of this life. There was a morning much like this one, only as far back as a month ago. I’d seen him as himself then, with that same wave, that same wanting. But now he wasn’t anywhere, and it makes me ashamed to say I feel less of that darkness now than I did then, the day after we lost him. Tommy isn’t anywhere on the hillside. I stand only with the lesser wound and the tears that come despite it. I allow my feet to carry me back to the car, to head back into town for the night, with the hope that no one there knows my name.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: I was thinking about the rubbish, the flapping plastic in the branches, the shoreline of odd boots and bottled drinks along the banks of the little stream, and for a moment my thoughts segued to the people walking towards the Lost Corner, looking for all the world like they were out for a stroll. So I stopped and waited, the wind tugging with the odd gust through my hair, and just for the frustration of it all, of how my plans had been disrupted, I imagined that all the things I had lost in life had washed up here on this spot. In front of me, on the horizon, he came trudging towards me with that odd gait he had. He was waving and laughing, as if this was a little slice of fun, and I wanted to cry out "Tommy," but I didn't, and he came on, so happy and fun, and I could feel the tears welling up. But then I reeled it back, let the fantasy unwind, and just stood in my normal stance, blinking into the wind. When I felt ready, I got in the car and went on with my life.
