written_by_MFA001.Original: We could have it for a month, she told me over the phone. Not that I think I’ll need that much time.Would I ever get used to this kind of talk? Even as I wondered what to do about my mail—let it pile up, have the post office forward it or hold it for me—I found it unthinkable to ask how long I should plan to be gone.It’s not like I’ve picked a date, she said. Though, as I say, I am ready to go. You could even say I’m impatient to go, which comes partly from my having already given so much thought to dying but also from having reached the limits of what I think I can bear. But I don’t know what my body will do.Though she’d been feeling much better since she went off chemo, her symptoms could change from day to day, and the meds she was taking to suppress them had some side effects too.In any case, I want things to happen naturally, she said. I feel like I’ll know when it’s time.But you—well, you won’t know, she said. Obviously I won’t be making a big announcement. Like the coming of the Lord, she said jokingly: You will not know the day or hour.She had decided not to tell anyone about our plans. I’ve come this far, I don’t want to risk some stupid intervention, she said, or even a tiny disruption. I want peace.No one was to know where we were.And, for your own protection, she told me, you need to play dumb: I never told you what I was going to do, you weren’t even aware that I had the drug.I had, in fact, already told one other person everything, but I did not say this.

written_by_MFA001.Excerpt1: I’m ready now, my friend said, and I said nothing because I didn't know what to say. There were ways people did these sorts of things, she explained to me, certain drugs people used. But she couldn't tell me which drugs. For my protection. Protection against what?, I wondered, but I didn't ask her. That seemed wrong to say. I wanted to ask her about when she was planning on taking these drugs, exactly, but I worried that line of questioning was unthinkable, morbid. I didn't want it to seem like I wanted a date so I could put it on my calendar and plan around it. Already, though, I was thinking about my plans. The mail stacking in the mailbox with each day I stayed with my friend. You don't have to tell me anything you don't want to, I said -- and then I worried that made it sound like I didn't really want to hear anything at all. But she just said, this way it's all in my hands. Her hands: frail, slightly shaking. She was ready to die, she told me, she wanted to get it over with, it felt like that was the way her body was heading. All the ups and downs with the treatments just delaying the inevitable. She was bound to die, just like the coming of the Lord was bound to happen, she said. She glanced upwards and my eyes followed hers. Nothing and no one appeared, and she looked back at me. Just promise you won't tell anyone, she said. I won't, I said -- it was a lie. The weight of the secret was too great. Her plans were too great, too serious. I didn't know what to do. I had already told someone else.
written_by_MFA001.Excerpt2: Look. I've been the one making the plan, and I want to be the one to execute it. There was a silence before she spoke again. I'll be honest, I'm not the kind of person who's so crazy about living that I want to put off dying as long as I possibly can. I'll be ready. In fact, I'm already impatient. But like I told you, no one can be sure how the cancer's going to behave. We all know there are sometimes surprises, and the body can be very stubborn about giving up, and it's always possible that treatment might be delayed. And I want this as natural as possible. I want to be in a certain state. I don't want to be in distress. I don't want to be rescued. I don't want my hand held. I'm sorry, but I just can't commit to any particular moment, any particular day. It could happen tomorrow. It could happen in a couple of weeks. As the saying goes, it'll be like the coming of the Lord. You won't know the day or the hour. But don't worry, she added, feeling the words catch in her throat. You'll know the minute afterward. Remembering my full mailbox, I said I'd want my mail held if I went away for a week or more. She pressed her lips together and frowned. I had gone too far. The truth was, it was unthinkable for me to bring all this up at all. I'd rather you didn't mention the drug, or how I got it, to anyone. You understand, don't you? For your own protection—and for mine. But this promise I had already broken. I had already shared this information with someone.

Hell, count them few times we been together in the same damn place. I got a gutful of it, enough. I'm done bein' dumb about this, see? When the hell we gonna get a chance to get it right? We been a fuckin' pair! And you know damn well what I'm sayin'. Damn you, Ennis del Mar. Brokeback Mountain—we kill ourselves up there. That's all we've got. Damn you. You've got me on a short leash, hung me up for years. Sometimes I miss you so much I can hardly stand it. I wish I knew how to quit you." Tears were running down Jack's face.Like vast, powerful haymakers, these words were blows that knocked a man down without warning. Ennis sagged to his knees seeking  to catch his breath. "Jesus," said Jack, thinking the man was having a heart attack as he knelt beside Ennis on the poured slab, putting his arm around his shoulder. Once the shock had passed Ennis hauled himself to his feet, flinched away from Jack, turned his back to him, and tried to be calm. He lit a cigarette, unbuckled his belt, and pulled his shirt out of his jeans. Nothing changed except who they were and what they felt—a silence that rose between them like clouds of steam.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: “You the storm that stranded me here,” said Jack. “Ain’t no other way to put it. I been thinkin on it, bustin my brain to try and fit the bits together, but it’s bullshit. You know it is, Ennis, don’t pretend like you don’t. I’ve called you, sent you letters first class, and you actin like the offseason applies to us. Brokeback’s just a little vacation, a couple ranch-hands in heat. Maybe you like it like that. You sure got me on a short leash. That’s all I am to you, Ennis: a bitch for the summer. I’d swallow glass if it meant I could spend the rest a my life on Brokeback, but you won’t even pick up the goddam phone.” Jack looked at the ridgeline. “I wish I knew how to quit you.” Ennis got down on one knee, and for a second Jack thought he was tying his shoe. Sobs wracked his ribs. “Jesus!” yelled Jack. Ennis kept crying. He looked down at the earth, the denim of his knee stirring up dust. To Jack he looked like a wounded horse, its hooves at rest. He feared for Ennis, this man for whom he had stored up so much love and hate. A cold distant man making a scene on the roadside—it didn’t make much in the way of sense. Jack had more to say but his jaw stayed shut. Ennis sobbed. After awhile he went still. Ennis pulled himself to his feet and pushed the dust off his jeans. Jack looked at him and Ennis looked back, but there was nothing there. Just the clouds of steam rising.
written_by_MFA012.Reason: Excerpt 1 better matches the sense of someone who knows their own emotions but can't quite articulate them fully and so resorts to profanities and the vernacular. There is some of that in Excerpt 2 but its strange observations - such as Ennis looking like a wounded horse - feel like a different character.
written_by_MFA012.Original: “Try this one,” said Jack, “and I’ll say it just one time. Tell you what, we could a had a good life together, a fuckin real good life. You wouldn’t do it, Ennis, so what we got now is Brokeback Mountain. Everything built on that. It’s all we got, boy, fuckin all, so I hope you know that if you don’t never know the rest. Count the damn few times we been together in twenty years. Measure the fuckin short leash you keep me on, then ask me about Mexico and then tell me you’ll kill me for needin it and not hardly never gettin it. You got no fuckin idea how bad it gets. I’m not you. I can’t make it on a couple a high-altitude fucks once or twice a year. You’re too much for me, Ennis, you son of a whoreson bitch. I wish I knew how to quit you.”Like vast clouds of steam from thermal springs in winter the years of things unsaid and now unsayable—admissions, declarations, shames, guilts, fears—rose around them. Ennis stood as if heart-shot, face grey and deep-lined, grimacing, eyes screwed shut, fists clenched, legs caving, hit the ground on his knees.“Jesus,” said Jack. “Ennis?” But before he was out of the truck, trying to guess if it was heart attack or the overflow of an incendiary rage, Ennis was back on his feet and somehow, as a coat hanger is straightened to open a locked car and then bent again to its original shape, they torqued things almost to where they had been, for what they’d said was no news. Nothing ended, nothing begun, nothing resolved.

Brokeback’s just a little vacation, a couple ranch-hands in heat. Maybe you like it like that. You sure got me on a short leash. That’s all I am to you, Ennis: a bitch for the summer. I’d swallow glass if it meant I could spend the rest a my life on Brokeback, but you won’t even pick up the goddam phone.” Jack looked at the ridgeline. “I wish I knew how to quit you.” Ennis got down on one knee, and for a second Jack thought he was tying his shoe. Sobs wracked his ribs. “Jesus!” yelled Jack. Ennis kept crying. He looked down at the earth, the denim of his knee stirring up dust. To Jack he looked like a wounded horse, its hooves at rest. He feared for Ennis, this man for whom he had stored up so much love and hate. A cold distant man making a scene on the roadside—it didn’t make much in the way of sense. Jack had more to say but his jaw stayed shut. Ennis sobbed. After awhile he went still. Ennis pulled himself to his feet and pushed the dust off his jeans. Jack looked at him and Ennis looked back, but there was nothing there. Just the clouds of steam rising.

written_by_MFA024.Excerpt1: Kant wrote thirty versions of his coming-out email over the course of ten months. Though he knew better, he couldn’t keep from anticipating and meticulously addressing, in the email itself, the various surprised, dismissive, or condemnatory responses of his friends and family, to the point where the email was less an act of claiming his own reality than a bullish bracing of himself against an incoming bilgewater tide of others’ realities. He clicked send. Feeling noble, self-satisfied, and above all ready, he camped at his laptop with an energy drink and spammed refresh. A couple hours later, an email from his father sent a spike of fear into his chest: he was about to be disowned. But while not exactly celebratory, the message indicated uncomplicated respect and acceptance. An email from an old college friend came in next, composed only of emojis. Where was their disgust? Their bitterness and disdain? The underwhelm was itself an overwhelm: he felt ridiculous, mocked by precisely an absence of mockery. Coming out should feel like something, shouldn’t it? He considered, by way of analogy, his own naïve expectation every birthday that he might experience an inner shift adequate to the day’s significance, a radiance, a spiritual lift, some kind of internal popping sound at least—I’m twenty-nine!—and instead met again and again just another day. Wasn’t this exactly how all life’s big events felt? A non-feeling? Supportive replies rolled in, and each refused to move the plot of his life forward. He’d imagined that this one symbolic action would release something huge and wild in him, that he’d start going on dates, he’d kiss the real flesh of a real guy; but months later he was still eating the same Cheez-Its and masturbating to the same porn, only now he didn’t even bother to clean up after himself. What he’d imagined calling The Year of Freedom had become The Year of Damp Feet.
written_by_MFA024.Excerpt2: What happened was—well, a lot happened. It took him a full year of latent DELAYED_MAIL exponential backoff before he managed to send a taut, defensive email to a BCC list of family, friends, and coworkers, coming up with some bullshit Aristotelian lie about fairness and specifically that it's totally unfair to ever be in the closet at all. He sent it out in the early morning hours of his 31st birthday, then paced up and down his hallway imagining worst-case replies: "You're dead to me"; "My poor boy, where did we go wrong"; "The priest has offered to counsel you"; "It sounds like you're legitimizing pederasty" . . . all cathected to a schizo runway reel of potential future selves: talented softcore pornographer with an 80-inch TV crashed out depressed on a couch with his own green-tinted face reflected in the screen; or candle-hoarding Toronto shut-in in a stuffed-animal bramble; or solitary defiant hedonist having foolish condomless sex and convicted of murder based on DNA evidence. He finally counted 18 breaths and, to delay longer, opened up a new doc and composed the marriage proposal he'd send to the first man to make him cum without dildos or videos. But when the replies in fact trickled in over the next week, they amounted to just kind of a turbocharged Like button: heart emojis from friends, who'd long since silently clocked him; two muted "God Blessings" from his coworkers; "well, okay then" from his mom, never to be remarked upon again; gentle wary "be the man you say you are" commandments from his dad. Whatever it was he'd been braced for, stinging recriminations and painful confessions to surmount over time, they never came, and so he never got to surmount them in a glorious montage. All he got instead was inertia and the Year of Damp Feet, and to be honest, though the relief was there, there was also, to be honest, a little bit of perverse disappointment.

written_by_MFA024.Original: It takes Kant a year to write the one-paragraph mass email, another three weeks to compile the Coming Out mailing list of friends, family, and colleagues, and three bourbons to actually send it. For his entire life he has so grotesquely imagined the consequences of public exposure that he’s only recently, at thirty-one, stopped hedging to himself that he is bi or “flexible.” He pictures his mother saying she never wants to speak to him again; he imagines dying alone in an unheated tenement, though he knows this is unlikely to happen to a video-game asset designer with two degrees. Part of him had believed that as long as his proclivities resided only in his head, and sometimes on his computer, they didn’t “count.” Now everyone will know; his sexuality will exist as an open fact. After sending the email, he turns off his phone and spends the night vomiting from stress.But the response is unanimously supportive. His friends reply with the visible spectrum of heart emojis. His coworkers politely underreact (“Oh neat! Psyched for you”). Kant’s parents are not thrilled exactly—they wish he’d called them first, though he couldn’t fathom doing this twice—yet they are neither disapproving nor surprised. The recent legalization of gay marriage probably helped; mainly his parents want to know whether he still plans on having kids, and he says yes, just to give them something.Perversely he sort of wishes the response had been more dramatic and adverse, to give him something to overcome, forcing growth in the process, though he knows he doesn’t really want that. But having tailored his life to compensate for its lack of relationships, there’s nothing compelling him to act on his new freedom, and instead he’s masturbating more than ever. He will recall this post-coming-out phase of his life as the Year of Damp Feet, spent forever popping into the shower to rinse off his dick and stomach.

But having tailored his life to compensate for its lack of relationships, there’s nothing compelling him to act on his new freedom, and instead he’s masturbating more than ever. written_by_MFA011.Original: It takes Kant a year to write the one-paragraph mass email, another three weeks to compile the Coming Out mailing list of friends, family, and colleagues, and three bourbons to actually send it. For his entire life he has so grotesquely imagined the consequences of public exposure that he’s only recently, at thirty-one, stopped hedging to himself that he is bi or “flexible.” He pictures his mother saying she never wants to speak to him again; he imagines dying alone in an unheated tenement, though he knows this is unlikely to happen to a video-game asset designer with two degrees. Part of him had believed that as long as his proclivities resided only in his head, and sometimes on his computer, they didn’t “count.” Now everyone will know; his sexuality will exist as an open fact. After sending the email, he turns off his phone and spends the night vomiting from stress.But the response is unanimously supportive. His friends reply with the visible spectrum of heart emojis. His coworkers politely underreact (“Oh neat! Psyched for you”). Kant’s parents are not thrilled exactly—they wish he’d called them first, though he couldn’t fathom doing this twice—yet they are neither disapproving nor surprised. The recent legalization of gay marriage probably helped; mainly his parents want to know whether he still plans on having kids, and he says yes, just to give them something.Perversely he sort of wishes the response had been more dramatic and adverse, to give him something to overcome, forcing growth in the process, though he knows he doesn’t really want that. But having tailored his life to compensate for its lack of relationships, there’s nothing compelling him to act on his new freedom, and instead he’s masturbating more than ever. He will recall this post-coming-out phase of his life as the Year of Damp Feet, spent forever popping into the shower to rinse off his dick and stomach.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: I breathed in the night air that might or might not have smelled like blossoms. Looking at the incomparable skyline of Manhattan, I felt a familiar thrill - one I'd never been able to explain, though I knew it came from seeing those tiny illuminated windows set against the massive forms that contained them.The thrill was so intense and singular that it must have been more than just the visual relationship, for apart from a cityscape, nothing natural or man-made held my attention long enough to provoke it. What I saw, I thought, was a material form of the second person plural, the true subject of art. It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. I'd long felt that one wanted to be an artist to make bad forms of collectivity appear as the promise of an almost unimaginable good: not reified abstraction, poorly disguised negation of the one in the many, but the emerging collective that would do justice to the wrongs absorbed by the bodies below the skyline. Tonight the fiction of the world—all my strongest perceptions, including rare fictions of participation in a benevolent collectivity—had gathered around Noor as if she were a black hole. Through her I was being changed more fully into a thing, a person among persons, and the experience was only horrible to the extent that it wasn't total. The uncanny feeling of not being identical with yourself, of being a stranger to your own experience, is profoundly alienating, yet it holds a glimmer of utopian hope. This sense of dislocation is available to be felt as a rearticulation, a promise that the past can be unlocked in the present. It is the paradoxical hope that in the moment you realize you are not yourself, you experience the possibility of becoming another, allowing the past to be reconfigured, rewritten in the now.I thought all this at midnight on a cheap folding bench with my hair flattened by a bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, tearing up a little—a mild lacrimal event—projecting myself into this scene from the future.
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?

Excerpt 2, on the other hand, seems more intent on philosophically waning about the comparison of the actual city components to the architecture of the Greeks and the Muslims, rather than the original and Excerpt 1, which talk about the authors emotional connection and response to the city scape.
written_by_MFA012.Original: I breathed in the night air that was or was not laced with anachronistic blossoms and felt the small thrill I always felt to a lesser or greater degree when I looked at Manhattan’s skyline and the innumerable illuminated windows and the liquid sapphire and ruby of trafﬁc on the FDR Drive and the present absence of the towers. It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

written_by_MFA012.Excerpt1: Gazing upon the skyline of Manhattan, I inhaled the stench of the sewers, the smoke of the gyro stand, and the fragrance of blossoms. For me, steel landscapes always followed this progression: first coarseness, then delectability, then something more subtly appetizing. The longer I looked, the more thrilling the tableau revealed itself to be, with the yellowed hued windows forming a jagged arcade. The buildings were so immense that I didn’t think of mountains so much as other buildings, particularly the skyscrapers-in-progress I had recently encountered in an architecture magazine. Granite ranges—not to mention waterfalls, alluvial plains, verdant valleys, desert mesas, and the like—have seldom made an impression on me. Yet this skyline, being the result of over a century of steel-hewn collective striving, provoked a deeper recognition; in the risings and falls of the rooftops, I pinpointed a material beyond that which the builders had worked with—something all-encompassing, a “you” to which a work of art would surely be addressed. Perhaps every work of art in the history of humankind—from the verses of Sappho, to the triumphs of Muslim architecture, to brush strokes of the Dutch masters, to the Goldberg Variations—had been addressed to this “you.” All the bundled debt of midtown was merely a muse to a Greek woman’s pen; pigments intermingled in the city water supply with the traces of antidepressants; the gridlock on the Brooklyn Bridge recalled the stylings of Ibn Tulun. Did the fog setting in over the river contain a hint of Bach? I couldn’t quite tell. Yet it didn’t matter: the world was a sprawling racket of collaboration, full of bad forms of collectivity which, as an artist, I could transform into something more, a brighter “you.” Of course, at that moment, as I meditated on the skyline, Noor insinuated herself into my thoughts. It was only natural, considering how the fiction of the world swarmed around her. As I sat on the bench, I almost felt as if I was sitting upon Noor, upon “you.” My consciousness waned into another—and was this such a crime? One could not be identical with oneself—but could one be better? After reaffixing my bandana to my head, and consuming an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, I found myself suffering a mild lacrimal event. Would the world make a skyline within you? Would we ever be a part of the human tangle?
written_by_MFA012.Excerpt2: I breathed in the night air that might or might not have smelled like blossoms. Looking at the incomparable skyline of Manhattan, I felt a familiar thrill - one I'd never been able to explain, though I knew it came from seeing those tiny illuminated windows set against the massive forms that contained them.The thrill was so intense and singular that it must have been more than just the visual relationship, for apart from a cityscape, nothing natural or man-made held my attention long enough to provoke it. What I saw, I thought, was a material form of the second person plural, the true subject of art. It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. I'd long felt that one wanted to be an artist to make bad forms of collectivity appear as the promise of an almost unimaginable good: not reified abstraction, poorly disguised negation of the one in the many, but the emerging collective that would do justice to the wrongs absorbed by the bodies below the skyline. Tonight the fiction of the world—all my strongest perceptions, including rare fictions of participation in a benevolent collectivity—had gathered around Noor as if she were a black hole. Through her I was being changed more fully into a thing, a person among persons, and the experience was only horrible to the extent that it wasn't total. The uncanny feeling of not being identical with yourself, of being a stranger to your own experience, is profoundly alienating, yet it holds a glimmer of utopian hope. This sense of dislocation is available to be felt as a rearticulation, a promise that the past can be unlocked in the present. It is the paradoxical hope that in the moment you realize you are not yourself, you experience the possibility of becoming another, allowing the past to be reconfigured, rewritten in the now.I thought all this at midnight on a cheap folding bench with my hair flattened by a bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, tearing up a little—a mild lacrimal event—projecting myself into this scene from the future.

written_by_MFA027.Excerpt2: The scent of blossoms colors the night, and New York in its entirety fits very neatly and completely into my hands. For instance, between my thumb and my index, lights flicker on and off in a miniature window. If I elongate my fingers I could also hold the silver skyscrapers tearing into the clouds. How astonishing; the skyline’s ants and beasts fit right, and wrong, into my palms. Back in my father's village nothing, absolutely nothing, fit into my hands. There were no neat edges anywhere, no contrast, nothing for me to want to try to hold. In short, there is no place I feel less alone than here, alone on this bench in New York, where the skyline is ours, and we are the skyline, my eyes staring straight into the material manifestation of a second person plural. In the future, they will say this skyline was synonymous with every art, every intimate form that has ever, or will ever, exist. To say we are the skyline is to confirm a collective identity, to confirm a stake in what makes up the city's sublime marrow; bundled debt, traces of antidepressants in the water, traffic networks, and shifting weather patterns. As an artist it will be my mission to transmute bad forms of collectivity into a sculpture of the communal body of the future. There is something Noor said once, in response to my ideas about the fiction of the world, that I am desperately trying to forget. We were not speaking the way people speak, necessarily, but more like skies, or skylines, when a passing cloud whispered something about a mirror. The disembodied voice said one cannot recognize oneself and at once be identical with oneself. But one plus one plus one equals three, if my math is correct. So maybe we multiply, keep multiplying, and our past and present and future selves never leave, and maybe that is what Noor really meant when she said the world has no genre you can name. The midnight air does nothing to unflatten my hair beneath the bandana. I would mistake this moment for a dream if I had not just consumed an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, the juice all over my fingers. I vaguely remember a dream of myself as an old man, maybe an old woman, my fingers free of both tiny windows and the stain of fruit, and with this memory of the future I experience a mild lacrimal event, and I feel very alone, and very together.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt1: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.

It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. I'd long felt that one wanted to be an artist to make bad forms of collectivity appear as the promise of an almost unimaginable good: not reified abstraction, poorly disguised negation of the one in the many, but the emerging collective that would do justice to the wrongs absorbed by the bodies below the skyline. Tonight the fiction of the world—all my strongest perceptions, including rare fictions of participation in a benevolent collectivity—had gathered around Noor as if she were a black hole. Through her I was being changed more fully into a thing, a person among persons, and the experience was only horrible to the extent that it wasn't total. The uncanny feeling of not being identical with yourself, of being a stranger to your own experience, is profoundly alienating, yet it holds a glimmer of utopian hope. This sense of dislocation is available to be felt as a rearticulation, a promise that the past can be unlocked in the present. It is the paradoxical hope that in the moment you realize you are not yourself, you experience the possibility of becoming another, allowing the past to be reconfigured, rewritten in the now.I thought all this at midnight on a cheap folding bench with my hair flattened by a bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, tearing up a little—a mild lacrimal event—projecting myself into this scene from the future.

It was a thrill that only built space produced in me, never the natural world, and only when there was an incommensurability of scale—the human dimension of the windows tiny from such distance combining but not dissolving into the larger architecture of the skyline that was the expression, the material signature, of a collective person who didn’t yet exist, a still-uninhabited second person plural to whom all the arts, even in their most intimate registers, were nevertheless addressed. Only an urban experience of the sublime was available to me because only then was the greatness beyond calculation the intuition of community. Bundled debt, trace amounts of antidepressants in the municipal water, the vast arterial network of trafﬁc, changing weather patterns of increasing severity— whenever I looked at lower Manhattan from Whitman’s side of the river I resolved to become one of the artists who momentarily made bad forms of collectivity ﬁgures of its possibility, a proprioceptive ﬂicker in advance of the communal body. What I felt when I tried to take in the skyline—and instead was taken in by it—was a fullness indistinguishable from being emptied, my personality dissolving into a personhood so abstract that every atom belonging to me as good belonged to Noor, the ﬁction of the world rearranging itself around her. If there had been a way to say it without it sounding like presumptuous co-op nonsense, I would have wanted to tell her that discovering you are not identical with yourself even in the most disturbing and painful way still contains the glimmer, however refracted, of the world to come, where everything is the same but a little different because the past will be citable in all of its moments, including those that from our present present happened but never occurred. You might have seen me sitting there on the bench that midnight, my hair matted down from the bandanna, eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango, and having, as I projected myself into the future, a mild lacrimal event.

written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. I am alienated. And I am the alienator—I have no false pretenses about this. How ironic it feels, sometimes, to know that I am alone, and yet not even identical with myself. Is it foolish that I find some hope in that? That I think of Noor and I feel her and I smell the blossoms of the city night and I understand that the past and present are formless, shapeless, and can be reorganized, reimagined into something bigger? I sit here and I look at the skylight. It’s midnight, and I am on a bench that’s cold and, I think, slightly damp, though it’s hard to tell. My eyes are blurry with exhaustion, my hair flattened by that blue bandanna from Goodwill, and I am eating an irresponsible quantity of unsulfured mango from a Ziplock bag. My eyes begin to burn, a mild lacrimal event, as I think of all this possibility. My fingertips are slightly slippery, sugared from the fruit I’m eating.

What I saw, I thought, was a material form of the second person plural, the true subject of art. It was sublime, a plural subject, skyline as collective body coming into being, a body that didn't exist yet, something to which you could belong in the future and sometimes in the present tense. It only appeared solid, towering, but all the things that produced the sublime effects were bad: titanic banks bundling debt against the general welfare, measurable traces of antidepressants in the water supply, traffic networks poisoning the air, and ever-worsening storms. written_by_MFA008.Excerpt2: I inhale the night, which has the faint taste of blossoms hanging on it. I always found it thrilling to watch the city this way, how the illuminated windows on apartment buildings and offices cling together as parts of an expansive and profoundly intricate skyline. The beauty others find in a mountain, a valley, a crested hill, I find in looking at urban mosaics like these, like Manhattan, this grand forest of buildings and bridges and smoke and air. I find that nature feels too much like a singular entity, a crystalline cohesion, whereas urban landscapes feel like a second person plural, something that does not exist now, but exists only in the future, a future where everything, art and intimacy and joy and expansion, has room to breathe and move. It’s almost unbearable, the sublimity of the bundled debt, the anti-depressants that stream through urine and into the water supply, the light pollution, traffic in the sky and on the ground, all connecting to create something artful and strange and united. This is what I think of when I gaze at the skyline, how I will become an artist, one who transforms and reshapes bad modes of collectivity into the possibility for good, into a broad future where all entities can exist in the same body. I think of Noor—how can I not?— and my connection to her, her connection to us all, her large and shapeless body, which the fiction of the world organizes itself so perfectly around. I am alone. written_by_MFA007.Excerpt1: I was on my way to see the woman as a visitor, riding up in an elevator filled with doctors and nurses clutching clipboards, and patients doubled over in pain. "Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine is needed in the consulting room," an announcement came over the PA system. Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine, however, never showed his face.My purpose in visiting her was clear enough: I intended to meet with her, regain her trust, and convince her to let me see the bag put to its intended use one last time."Would you mind undoing the ends of the cord so I can check how you attached it?" "Would you like me to take a photograph of you wearing it?" "Do you need to have another hole punched in the strap to make it longer?" I rehearsed these lines in my head. I realized I had never spoken to her so politely.In truth, I simply needed to make her put the bag down for a moment. I planned to face her, extend to her all the gratitude I felt for having been allowed to sew the bag on. Then, once she let her guard down, I would press the shears to her chest. The shears were hidden, but soon she'd feel the cold steel pressed against her belly, slowly moving up toward her breasts. She'd moan in fear. I'd then carefully—oh so carefully—slice through the flesh as though cutting through layers of delicate silk. When the final thread had been cut and the heart was liberated from her chest, there would be no need anymore to smile and exchange pleasantries. The bag would be mine alone. But not because I wanted it. No, I was doing this to restore the proper order of things. I'd hold the bag in one hand and the shears in the other. The elevator finally climbed to the sixth floor.
written_by_MFA007.Excerpt2: The elevator opened onto the third floor, and I flattened myself against the side as a patient and his doctor exited. “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine,” said the intercom. On the fourth floor, two nurses entered the crowded elevator. As I was forced into the corner, I heard “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine” bleat over the intercom again. I had two more floors left before I’d reach hers. Whether Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine appeared or not, I had a plan, infallible and precise. I would see her, lying prone on her hospital bed, and hold up the bag. “I have to apologize for everything,” I’d say. “I made this bag for you. I crafted it myself.”“How lovely,” she’d respond, her voice lax from the painkillers. “How many pockets does it have?”“Six,” I’d say. “What material did you use to stitch it together?” “Cowhide. It feels like a baby’s cheek. Feel it,” I’d say. “Please, feel it.”When she reached out to touch her finger on the belly of the bag, I’d lean over and, taking my shears out, throw away the hospital linens covering her body. Then, as her hand caressed the bag’s soft skin, I’d cut into her chest. I’d trim the strings of the heart first, the extraneous vessels and tissue that fastened it to her insides. Once it was freed, I’d toss the shears aside. Then I’d grasp it with my bare hand. In my palm, her heart would fit like a baseball. After it was done, I’d leave, my bag in hand, alone. “Dr Y. from Respiratory Medicine,” repeated the intercom. As another nurse shuffled past me, I clutched the bag to my chest. Its delicate construction couldn’t dull the shears hidden inside. Their blades were so sharp that, when the elevator moved upward once more, they pricked me. The elevator dinged for the sixth floor.

written_by_MFA007.Original: “Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine. Dr. Y from Respiratory Medicine. I was sure I’d be able to find her room. I would pretend I was just visiting her, or I could say I wanted her to pay me for the bag. After all, I ought to get something for all my work.First, I’ll apologize for the other day—very humbly, in order to regain her trust. And then I’ll say what I’ve come to say: “Making your bag has been a very important experience for me. I don’t think I’ll ever have the chance to make a piece like this again. But not because I wanted it. No, I was doing this to restore the proper order of things. I'd hold the bag in one hand and the shears in the other. The elevator finally climbed to the sixth floor.

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: To be a feminist — perhaps, to be a woman at all — is to teeter on the edge of a chasm between principle and performance. This week I rode the subway for the first time in months. In a moment of hyperperception, I swept my awareness over the scene: dusty bottles at the edge of the track, a lone rat scurrying into the bowels of the public transit system, three men hulking at one side of a gum-stained bench, blasting Drake on a tinny speaker. I found myself acutely aware not only of my perception of the scene, but of the men’s perception of my perception of the scene, and my perception of the men’s perception of my perception. Was I to admonish these men for listening to an artist well-known for wrapping misogyny in a catchy tune and feeding it to vulnerable audiences of young, troubled men? Did they expect this of me —were they waiting for my reprimand, already preparing their rebuttal? Should I be bracing myself for a flurry of calm downs and lighten ups? I did none of these things. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for wearing pink flowy maxi dresses that highlight my femininity, a choice in line with the beauty standards and fashion requirements long used to subjugate women — to make women seem weaker, more delicate, more frivolous. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for ceding, at times, to this perception of the feminine as frail and foolish when it conveniences me: allowing a gallant male stranger to change my tire on the side of the road or letting my professional persona slip in a rare moment of vulnerability. Perhaps I am a bad feminist for thinking any of this at all — by discounting my true nature, I am participating in the classic erasure of women’s personal desires in favor of the welfare of others. Perhaps I am a bad feminist. But I am also a tired feminist. Where does it end? Am I to be trapped forever in this infinite moral calculation of every action and every thought? Candidly, I don’t mind being a bad feminist, if it means I can be like the subway rat — revolting and dirty, maybe, but free to scurry at my whim.

written_by_MFA026.Excerpt2: At one time I imagined that being a desirable woman made you an object and being an undesirable woman made you a person. In the years since I’ve learned that being an undesirable woman actually makes you less than a person, makes you something subhuman. If you are a woman but not a beautiful woman, are instead a fat woman scorned by men and more largely scorned by a society that understands women as objects subjected to male desire, then you are not allowed to be human. And this is me. Not quite a human because of the body I live in. This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. The thin woman is a woman who is allowed to be a woman. These fantasies border phantasmagoria, bad feminist rhetoric equating internal change with external corroboration. What does it mean, then, if I long for independence and long also to be cared for, to surrender to care. If I want to present myself as a professional and want also to be vulnerable, to handle my vulnerability as a weapon. This, too, tied with physicality—to want to look like woman, wear pink and enjoy fashion, and simultaneously live as a professional who critiques beauty standards asking women to starve themselves into shadows and silhouettes. I might listen to rap with inherently anti-feminist lyrics, I might wear pink skirts and loathe maxi dresses made for thin bodies and thin bodies alone, and I might hate myself for all this—I may find myself mortified by these choices, by the bad feminist implications therein. But none of this posturing, none of these feelings, exempt me from the womanhood I was born into. There is no good feminist, I could argue. There is no way out. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

This realm is where my own bad feminism is seen again and again, in my understanding that there is no right way to be a woman, no way to be a woman and live an uncomplicated human existence, put in conflict with a desire to be a woman who is allowed to be. When I think about weight loss, about changing myself so that I might live in an uncontroversial body, I see in this transformation some proof of concept: if I can be normal, if I can be accepted in my body, then my life will be made significantly simpler. If you want to be human, you cannot also be a woman.

written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. written_by_MFA002.Excerpt1: My awkward undergraduate years are better left undiscussed, but lately I have found myself turning them over in my head in search of an insight that has eluded me since – what drove me to join my university’s chapter of the Black Panther Party? Ostensibly I supported the movement and its ideologies, but in retrospect – and in all honesty – my desire to resist the oppression of my people was, perhaps, not the most pertinent factor in my decision. Really I joined the Party as a means of proving myself – more specifically, proving my Blackness. And to whom was this posturing directed? Certainly at the white and Black basketball players alike who laughed me off the court when I mumbled “Egads” upon a fumbled shot. Certainly at Todd Henderson, the literary critic who called my retelling of Aeschylus’s Prometheus Bound “disconcertingly cerebral” for an author like me. And candidly, perhaps at myself. I needed to convince myself that I was Black enough. And maybe I still do, decades later. The other day I attended a literary party in the city and somehow found myself sucked into a conversation with an agent of an acquaintance. “Don’t bother with the Achilles,” the agent told me. (Privately I considered correcting his pronunciation of Aeschylus, then decided it wasn’t worth the effort.) “It’s not what they want. They’re looking for true, gritty, real stories of Black life. They want authenticity.” This puzzled me. I asked him to define authentic. What makes me, a Black man writing material guided by my lived experience, not authentically Black? To this, the agent laughed, clapped me on the shoulder, and moved on to debate the prevalence of body shaming in social media with a bemused performance artist perusing the hors d’oeuvres. Today, as I write, I consider my opinion on it all – Blackness, whiteness, authenticity. I don’t really believe in race. I regard race as a construct of convenience, a societal demarcation on which I rarely dwell. And yet, I recognize the self-indulgent folly in the popular adage, I don’t see color. I am not blind to the concrete consequences of racial divides: oppression, discrimination, violence, subjugation. But there’s something artificial and contrived about the Blackness that I feel I must actively demonstrate.
written_by_MFA002.Excerpt2: When I was in college I joined the Black Panther Party. I wore a black turtleneck sweater and black beret and stood outside in the cold with arms full of old newspapers. I wasn’t trying to prove my ideological stance. I was trying to prove that I was indeed Black. It seems that no one, Black or white, thought I was Black enough. Once when a loose ball was bounding about on a basketball court, I muttered “Egads,” and people’s heads turned. When I savored a biscuit and described it as sublime, I received odd looks. And, of course, I was not nearly gloomy or angry enough as a writer. Of a retelling of Aeschylus, a reviewer wrote: “The novel has some merit, but do we really need this from a Black man?” A literary agent puffed up with plastic pride told me at a New York party that nobody wanted an intellectual Black man, especially one doing retellings of Greek plays. I pointed out that I actually knew Greek. He laughed and asked if that was a joke and suggested I should write some true, gritty real stories of Black life instead. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories. I was sure that he had no idea what I was talking about.He sniffed at the air, feigned boredom and proceeded to chat up the Afro woman, who I heard later was a performance artist. I knew I was Black, saw myself as Black, but race was a fiction. A handy one, a stupid one, a dangerous one, but a fiction nonetheless. To be honest I don’t think about race much, except when my liberal guilt compels me to consider it or when I read about some thirteen-year-old kid being shot by some cop, and then I remember that though race is a construct without a basis in the natural world, those bullets are quite real and deadly.

Both Blacks and whites alike told me that I was "not Black enough" for them (they saw the way I played basketball, muttering "Egads" under my breath with every foul or missed layup—Egads). This applied not only to my physical appearance and manner of speech but also extended to my intellect and my books.My most recent manuscript was denied by every major publisher. From a reviewer: "While somewhat compelling and an interesting take on the retelling of Aeschylus, we just don't see how it relates to the Black experience." Despite my being a Black writer, the book was, apparently, not written from a Black perspective. At the latest New York literary party, a well-known literary agent told me, "You should forget those retellings of yours; classical works aren't what the market is looking for. What we're seeking are the true, gritty stories of Black life—write that, then give me a call."I told him, "My stories are Black stories." And in their own way, it was true. Was I not a Black writer? The agent shuffled past me to attend to a performance artist so they could see what they could do for one another, before never speaking to each other again.I didn't know how to contend with any of it: how to portray myself as "Black enough," the backward, ill-feeling guilt behind not being so, and how to fit into the mold that society made of Black men. We all had to be gangsters, rappers. But why should I have been anything other than who I was? Race was a construct I didn't believe in and rarely dwelt on, until those moments arose when guilt compelled me to see the "other side" of the matter. I saw its real-world consequences: police brutality, discrimination, violence. I didn't know if that meant I was supposed to take part in any of it.
written_by_MFA015.Excerpt2: When I was in college I joined the Black Panther Party. I wore a black turtleneck sweater and black beret and stood outside in the cold with arms full of old newspapers. I wasn’t trying to prove my ideological stance. I was trying to prove that I was indeed Black. It seems that no one, Black or white, thought I was Black enough. Once when a loose ball was bounding about on a basketball court, I muttered “Egads,” and people’s heads turned. When I savored a biscuit and described it as sublime, I received odd looks. And, of course, I was not nearly gloomy or angry enough as a writer. Of a retelling of Aeschylus, a reviewer wrote: “The novel has some merit, but do we really need this from a Black man?” A literary agent puffed up with plastic pride told me at a New York party that nobody wanted an intellectual Black man, especially one doing retellings of Greek plays. I pointed out that I actually knew Greek. He laughed and asked if that was a joke and suggested I should write some true, gritty real stories of Black life instead. He glanced across the room at a woman with strings of beads in her otherwise naked Afro, then turned back to me. He said if I gave him a story about cocaine and drive-bys and baby mamas and regrets, he would make me a millionaire. I told him to fuck off and that my life was Black and that the stories I wrote were in fact Black stories. I was sure that he had no idea what I was talking about.He sniffed at the air, feigned boredom and proceeded to chat up the Afro woman, who I heard later was a performance artist. I knew I was Black, saw myself as Black, but race was a fiction. A handy one, a stupid one, a dangerous one, but a fiction nonetheless. To be honest I don’t think about race much, except when my liberal guilt compels me to consider it or when I read about some thirteen-year-old kid being shot by some cop, and then I remember that though race is a construct without a basis in the natural world, those bullets are quite real and deadly.

written_by_MFA015.Original: While in college I was a member of the Black Panther Party, defunct as it was, mainly because I felt I had to prove I was black enough. Some people in the society in which I live, described as being black, tell me I am not black enough. Some people whom the society calls white tell me the same thing. I have heard this mainly about my novels, from editors who have rejected me and reviewers whom I have apparently confused and, on a couple of occasions, on a basketball court when upon missing a shot I muttered Egads. From a reviewer: "The novel is finely crafted, with fully developed characters, rich language and subtle play with the plot, but one is lost to understand what this reworking of Aeschylus’ The Persians has to do with the African American experience.".One night at a party in New York, one of the tedious affairs where people who write mingle with people who want to write and with people who can help either group begin or continue to write, a tall, thin, rather ugly book agent told me that I could sell many books if I’d forget about writing retellings of Euripides and parodies of French poststructuralists and settle down to write the true, gritty real stories of black life. I told him that I was living a black life, far blacker than he could ever know, that I had lived one, that I would be living one. He left me to chat with an on-the-rise performance artist/novelist who had recently posed for seventeen straight hours in front of the governor’s mansion as a lawn jockey. He familiarly flipped one of her braided extensions and tossed a thumb back in my direction.The hard, gritty truth of the matter is that I hardly ever think about race. Those times when I did think about it a lot I did so because of my guilt for not thinking about it. I don’t believe in race. I believe there are people who will shoot me or hang me or cheat me and try to stop me because they do believe in race, because of my brown skin, curly hair, wide nose and slave ancestors. But that’s just the way it is.

written_by_MFA030.Excerpt1: I remember those college days. The grass peeking over cement, the columns of the buildings thick, stuffed, presumably, with knowledge. Though, admittedly, I had a hard time juggling it all, having joined the Panthers on campus, less for their social cause, and more to reject the budding questions about my Blackness. Needless to say, it didn't work. Everywhere I went, strangers, white and Black, would tell me I wasn't Black enough. The white friends wanted to know why I didn't keep a gun, like a real Black Panther, and the Panthers wanted to know why I was so busy doing the white man's homework. Once, an entire basketball court stopped the game to laugh for five minutes when they heard me mutter egads after missing a shot. I can take these teases in everyday life, but when it comes to my literature, that's when the blade cuts deepest. The most recent was a slack-mouthed reviewer who wondered why my last novel, a retelling of Aeschylus, did not portray adequately, as they put it, "the Black man's experience." This was no unusual comment. At a literary party, I was once told to abandon my passion for classic retellings in favor of "true, gritty real stories of Black life." There were millions to be made here, an agent had said. When I refused their suggestion, telling them that all of my stories are stories of Black life, because I, a Black life, made them, they moseyed over to a performance artist, with whom they spent the rest of the evening talking about sword-swallowing. I looked at the paintings on the walls of the luxury Harlem apartment, all of Black strife, contorted faces, hands in yearning, bodies that seldom looked like bodies. Pictures of poverty worth millions. I couldn't say that I believed in race at all - I saw it merely as a construct. And yet, its grasp over me and those around me felt crushing, inevitable, real. I knew if I burned the apartment to the ground, as I felt the growing desire to do, the newspaper would not say "Established Author Sets Party Ablaze in Fit of Misplaced Justice." No, it would simply say, "Black Man Commits Arson." That would be how I would be remembered.

written_by_MFA029.Excerpt1: Craving and its indulgence are really one and the same thing. There might be no fruits, and still, if one wished for them, yearned for them, one would taste them all. The very sight of a berry in the wild is an admonishment not to pick it, for when it is stored in the vision and played upon by desire, the taste it bears is gifted to it as much by memory as by its savor. The flavor grows until it is too exquisite for the tongue, unencumbered by flesh. So it is when one wishes for a friend, or a woman, or a child. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The wind was dying, the sun was sinking, the side of the house was cooling, the evening moths were glancing and settling, and her absence was a thing so full of longing it became a presence of its own. If I could row the lake at dawn and gather all the proud blossoms from the woods for one year, I would throw some across the graves of unsanctified and dreamless children and some into the holes of fox dens. And with the rest I would sculpt from snow a statue of a woman. I would stand her in the clearing in the woods, and she would be adorned with rare flowers with leaves like hands, with hardstem thistles, and the birds would rest in her. Lot's wife would have none of this: flowers in profusion and children. Her breast caved into a hollow of regret. Not this one, not my mother. All the wild children, who knew too well that the world does not give itself generously to children, would burst from the trees and behold her. And every child, the most orphaned, the most bereft, would forgive her for her frozen hands and would stand at her white hem in awe that she should seem to shower them with blossoms, eternally offering what she could never give, inexplicably so stern.
written_by_MFA029.Excerpt2: I’ve realized that craving and fulfillment are not connected in the way I once thought. A craving is so intense and visceral that it cannot be truly satiated by consuming the thing you want. For example, berries are always sweeter before I eat them. I wonder if that’s how Eve felt in the garden after she tasted the forbidden fruit—disappointed, hungry, running her tongue over her teeth in search of satisfaction. I’ve been thinking about Sylvie, and how she disappeared silently into the forest and left me alone. I suspected she might be hiding somewhere, watching from a perch atop a spruce tree or huddled inside a hollow log. She liked to tease me. I didn’t want to give her the satisfaction of calling out for her, making her think I was afraid of being alone. I didn’t want her to feel like she’d rescued me by returning. I meandered around the little clearing and looked at the great towering tree trunks and their long shadows and the patches of grass poking up from the dark earth. In the center of it all, I imagined a statue. She was carved from some kind of pale, luminescent stone, something that seemed to give off its own light from within. Rare flowers were twined in her hair—orchid doves, lenten roses, midnight clematis. Blossoming vines wound up her body, not trapping her, but protecting her. My statue was a radiant mother, utterly unlike the barren, remorseful wife of Lot. She was vibrant and forgiving, always surrounded by children who marveled at her quiet beauty. The children, wild vagabonds of the forest, would be drawn to her through some mysterious summons, and they would huddle before her and bask in her gentle solace. Though her frozen hands would never touch them, she would look upon them with a kindness they had never known, and their happy tears would feed the vines and flowers that had made her their home. When the children were with her, they were not orphans, but children who had been made to be loved by a mother.

written_by_MFA029.Original: To crave and to have are as like as a thing and its shadow. For when does a berry break upon the tongue as sweetly as when one longs to taste it, and when is the taste refracted into so many hues and savors of ripeness and earth, and when do our senses know any thing so utterly as when we lack it? And here again is a foreshadowing—the world will be made whole. For to wish for a hand on one’s hair is all but to feel it. So whatever we may lose, very craving gives it back to us again. Though we dream and hardly know it, longing, like an angel, fosters us, smooths our hair, and brings us wild strawberries.Sylvie was gone. She had left without a word, or a sound. I thought she must be teasing, perhaps watching me from the woods. I pretended not to know I was alone. I could see why Sylvie thought children might come here. Any child who saw once how the gleaming water spilled to the tips of branches, and rounded and dropped and pocked the softening shadows of frost at the foot of each tree, would come to see it again.If there had been snow I would have made a statue, a woman to stand along the path, among the trees. The children would have come close, to look at her. Lot’s wife was salt and barren, because she was full of loss and mourning, and looked back. But here rare flowers would gleam in her hair, and on her breast, and in her hands, and there would be children all around her, to love and marvel at her for her beauty, and to laugh at her extravagant adornments, as if they had set the flowers in her hair and thrown down all the flowers at her feet, and they would forgive her, eagerly and lavishly, for turning away, though she never asked to be forgiven. Though her hands were ice and did not touch them, she would be more than mother to them, she so calm, so still, and they such wild and orphan things.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: There are times when to long for something is almost as satisfying as to finally receive it, or when the essence of that which is desired is evoked so clearly that to receive it is no longer necessary. As when one yearns to pluck a berry from the vine and savor its ripeness, so that the sweetness seems to precede the taste of the juice itself. Sylvie had said earlier that in springtime we could pick berries here. I searched for Sylvie's hand beside mine, but I found that she had slipped away silently and left me alone in the clearing. Yet in some way, I felt I could sense her closeness and thought she might be watching me from the woods, so I showed no change in my expression and pretended to be ignorant of my solitude. Around me, the sun cast long shadows through the partings of the tree branches, from which the browned leaves had already begun to fall into the clearing. A thin layer of frost was formed on the mud around where I sat. I imagined forming out of this cold clay earth a statue of a woman whom I would adorn with rare flowers. She would be a calm presence standing among the trees, not the cold, hard pillar of salt into which Lot's wife was transformed as punishment for her desire, for turning back with regret to look at all she had lost. A figure free of yearning, around whom the wild children of the forest would gather to marvel at her beauty and warmth. They would take solace in the vivacious beauty of such a figure and cling to her almost as a mother, even as her frozen hands could not caress them as one would their own children. Again I looked for Sylvie and thought of how I was, in searching for someone who had left me, not unlike the poor woman who had been turned to salt. Unlike the taste of those imagined berries, I was not sure if my longing for connection could ever be quite enough to evoke the presence of the thing itself.

written_by_MFA005.Excerpt2: Craving and its indulgence are really one and the same thing. There might be no fruits, and still, if one wished for them, yearned for them, one would taste them all. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The flavor grows until it is too exquisite for the tongue, unencumbered by flesh. So it is when one wishes for a friend, or a woman, or a child. For Sylvie disappeared and made no sound, and I fancied when I had closed my eyes and rocked awhile that she was not gone. It was easier than I could have imagined to pretend I was not alone, to insist that she merely watched me from the woods. The wind was dying, the sun was sinking, the side of the house was cooling, the evening moths were glancing and settling, and her absence was a thing so full of longing it became a presence of its own. If I could row the lake at dawn and gather all the proud blossoms from the woods for one year, I would throw some across the graves of unsanctified and dreamless children and some into the holes of fox dens. And with the rest I would sculpt from snow a statue of a woman. I would stand her in the clearing in the woods, and she would be adorned with rare flowers with leaves like hands, with hardstem thistles, and the birds would rest in her. Lot's wife would have none of this: flowers in profusion and children. Her breast caved into a hollow of regret. Not this one, not my mother. All the wild children, who knew too well that the world does not give itself generously to children, would burst from the trees and behold her. And every child, the most orphaned, the most bereft, would forgive her for her frozen hands and would stand at her white hem in awe that she should seem to shower them with blossoms, eternally offering what she could never give, inexplicably so stern.
written_by_MFA009.Excerpt2: Sometimes I wonder about the difference between craving something and fulfillment. Sometimes I want something so much I feel like I’m going to break open. Let’s say it’s a fresh berry, let’s say it’s like I’ve been really wanting a fresh berry, plucked from a bush in the orchard, even before that berry’s in my hands, it’s already got a taste in my mind, I’ve been building it up moment after moment until I have it in my brain like I’ve already got it on my tongue, so when Sylvie tells me she picked something for me and plops it in my mouth, it’s even sweeter because the sweetness confirms the foundation I’ve already built for it. I don’t know how to put it. Sylvie disappeared for a while, like a mouse, but then she came back. Sometimes she still goes out though, vanishes into the woods without saying anything. I think she’s out there right now, watching me ruminate. I don’t know what kind of solitude we can both get when we both are in each other’s minds. Could it be a way of being together? A very strange way? It’s beautiful out in the woods. The trees are older than I can fathom, really, old like stories can be old. I’d like to put a status out there, almost like somebody would always be watching, a statue of a woman, to stand in between all those old trees, a woman in a crown of new flowers, looking only ever ahead, forward, never letting any kind of barrenness touch her, like she was the opposite of Lot’s wife and all there was to her was the kind of forgiving vibrancy that children wonder at, the vibrancy that comes from a life well-lived. Even as a statue, I think they’d come to her, every child that’s ever felt lost-wild and orphan, and I think when they’d reach out to touch her stone hands, they’d find that that statue’s stone was warm for them. Sometimes I wish Sylvie were warmer. There’s warmth all around in all the beautiful trees and even the grasses. The problem is that trees don’t feel warm when you touch their bark unless it’s from the sun.
